source.title: Attribution Patching Outperforms Automated Circuit Discovery
source.authors: Aaquib Syed; C. Rager; Arthur Conmy

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates attribution patching and ACDC circuit-recovery methods against the previously identified IOI circuit, and measures attribution scores for IOI circuit edge classes. These are conceptually related tests, not the original circuit's activation-patching faithfulness, completeness, or minimality tests.
record.gate_note: The IOI ROC results measure circuit recovery against a previously identified circuit, and Appendix E reports IOI attribution-score distributions by edge role. The docstring approximation results and Greater-Than results are for different tasks and are not included. The cited original IOI study is used as ground truth, not as a new result here.
record.test_reason: Different method on the same question. Figure 2a reports how closely EAP and ACDC (with two metrics) recover the published IOI circuit, which bears on V4. Appendix E reports first-order attribution scores by IOI head class, which bears weakly on V1's roles. The original faithfulness, completeness and minimality tests are not rerun.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also find that attribution patching approximates activation patching poorly on Docstring (R²=0.27), and they recommend running EAP first, then ACDC on the pruned graph. They state that human-found circuits are an imperfect ground truth.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses Edge Attribution Patching, a first-order approximation to activation patching, and evaluates circuit recovery using ROC curves against previously identified circuits. It also benchmarks ACDC with different metrics rather than retesting the original IOI circuit's faithfulness, completeness, and minimality criteria.
record.method_sensitivity: For IOI circuit recovery, ACDC's ROC AUC differs between the task-specific metric (0.588) and KL divergence (0.868).
record.peer_reviewed: BlackboxNLP Workshop on Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP (the paper text also identifies a NeurIPS 2023 ATTRIB Workshop)
record.problems: The IOI comparisons use a previously identified circuit as ground truth rather than independently validating the circuit's behavior. Appendix E reports attribution-score distributions, not direct activation-patching tests of all stated head roles. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the ROC AUC results.
record.rows_left_out: No IOI results relevant to the tested versions were left out. The paper's Docstring and Greater-Than circuit-recovery results and its Docstring attribution-versus-activation-patching analyses are excluded because they concern different tasks.

untested.parts: Faithfulness, completeness and minimality of the 26-head, 7-class circuit. Causal roles of the previous-token, duplicate-token, induction and S-inhibition classes.
All parts (backup name movers are not examined).
All parts (only GPT-2 small IOI is tested; the other tasks are separate circuits, not reuse).
Ablation types (mean vs resample). Whether the recovered circuits have the same head classes and roles, beyond edge-level ROC overlap.
All parts: faithfulness and completeness of the IOI circuit under different ablations, metrics or prompt distributions are not measured.
All parts (no name-order, template or more-names variants).

missing.what: IOI attribution scores, in-circuit vs out-of-circuit edges: in-circuit mean −0.0080 (sd 0.1063), out-of-circuit mean 0.0000 (sd 0.0061). Only 6 out-of-circuit edges lie outside ±0.25.

record.verdict_notes: This is a methods paper that uses the IOI circuit as ground truth. It is counted as testing V4 only because V4 is itself the claim that other methods recover the same circuit. No uncertainty is reported for the AUCs. The original circuit's ablation-based criteria are never rerun.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test the 26-head, 7-class circuit's faithfulness, completeness, or minimality by removing everything outside it. Appendix E examines attribution scores by edge class, not the original activation-patching interventions; it does not establish every class's stated causal role.
Backup heads taking over after main name-mover ablation are not examined.
The paper does not test whether the same IOI circuit operates across models, sizes, checkpoints, or other tasks.
It compares EAP and ACDC with different metrics on IOI circuit recovery, but does not compare multiple ablation types or establish that the recovered circuits have the same components and roles.
IOI recovery performance is compared across metrics. Prompt-distribution sensitivity and the claim that the circuit explains only part of IOI behavior are not tested.
Other name orders, templates, and prompts with more names are not tested.

rows.operation_detail: Measured attribution scores for edges classified as Previous Token
rows.measure: Attribution score distribution; mean and standard deviation
rows.uncertainty: std=0.0566 (distribution standard deviation, not an error estimate)
rows.note: The authors describe this class's attribution scores as centered around zero; the score distribution alone does not establish its causal role under activation patching.
rows.check: Linear attribution scores are pooled over all edges leaving these heads. On Docstring, the paper reports they correlate only weakly with activation patching (R²=0.27). A near-zero mean cannot show the class's causal role.
